records.name: Central Visayas
records.current_summary:
Central Visayas holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside the capital region. Mandaue City signed the Implementation Rules and Regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024, formalised jointly with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and a UN development programme — an operational, not merely symbolic, local protection in the Cebu metro. The municipality of Carmen, northern Cebu, approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance protecting people on SOGIE grounds by unanimous Sangguniang Bayan vote in June 2025, days before the end of Pride month.

No killings, assaults or institutional-hostility incidents specific to trans visitors or residents are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national violence series or elsewhere in the research record. A visitor in Cebu/Mandaue can invoke an operational anti-discrimination ordinance — protection without any accompanying regional violence signal.

sources.claim: UNDP Philippines press release: Mandaue City strengthened protection against LGBTQ discrimination — the July 2024 signing of the Anti-Discrimination Ordinance's implementing rules and regulations with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and UNDP. (Record URL blocked automated fetch with an Access Denied page; summary from the research dossier line.)

mytv.ph local news: a town in northern Cebu passed a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance days before the end of Pride Month, safeguarding against SOGI-based discrimination - municipal-level protection inside Central Visayas; extractable text limited to the article header (exact date/town not recoverable).

records.name: Soccsksargen
records.current_summary:
In June 2025, transgender-rights activist Ali Jejhon Macalintal was shot dead in General Santos City. Human Rights Watch called the killing an “apparent targeted killing” and said police were examining her activism as a possible motive. The national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as “marked by cruelty and impunity” — the strongest official wording in this record for any region — and named Macalintal.

No protective ordinance or institutional counterweight is documented in this region, and the killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources. For a trans visitor the finding is targeted lethal violence against activists in a province with an official acknowledgement of impunity and no local machinery to answer it.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch statement (June 2025) on the murdered trans-rights activist in the Philippines: Macalintal's General Santos shooting as an apparent targeted killing and police examining her activism as a motive. (Record URL is a rewritten, 404-returning variant of the cited HRW address and the cached copy captured only site navigation; content per the research dossier.)

Philippine daily report (27 June 2025): the Commission on Human Rights condemns the killings of two transgender women as marked by cruelty and impunity, naming Macalintal. (Publisher returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary from the research dossier line.)

sources.title: Recent killings of trans women prompt groups to push for LGBTQIA protection (Bulatlat, 26 June 2025)
sources.claim: Bulatlat report (Dominic Gutoman, 26 June 2025): on 23 June 2025 an unidentified gunman killed trans woman and former journalist-activist Ali Macalintal inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos City; Macalintal was a former deputy secretary general of Karapatan-Soccsksargen Region and a former anchor-reporter of Radio Philippines Network DXDX-General Santos City. Bahaghari decried the killing and also reported the earlier killing of trans woman Shalani Dolina in Caloocan, and the piece notes no national anti-discrimination statute exists, with the SOGIESC Equality Bill stuck in Congress for 25 years. Region-naming source that independently confirms the General Santos City killing and Macalintal's own Soccsksargen-based activism role that this record's summary claims.

sources.title: Call us by our names: Trans Filipinos demand legal gender recognition (Rappler MovePH, 3 July 2025)
sources.claim: Rappler MovePH piece (3 July 2025): during Pride Month the Commission on Human Rights called the string of killings of transgender women a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide', citing human rights advocate Ali Macalintal being shot inside an acupuncture clinic (General Santos) alongside 18-year-old student Kierra Apostol and the earlier gunning down of beauty salon owner Ren Tampus; groups used the killings to push the Simplified Legal Gender Recognition Bill, with CHR's Fayda M. Dumarpa pledging support. Major-media confirmation that the Macalintal killing in General Santos is officially framed as part of a national transfemicide pattern, corroborating this record's claim of official acknowledgement without a protective institutional answer.

records.name: Central Luzon
records.current_summary:
Angeles City and the Clark-Subic corridor in Pampanga constitute the region's principal traveler-facing risk. In June 2025 the National Bureau of Investigation's Bataan District Office dismantled a trafficking operation at Field Sensation's Bar in Angeles City, arresting four people and rescuing 45 victims including 13 minors; in March 2025 the same office arrested a foreign national and accomplices in Angeles City under the Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act, rescuing 12 victims including 5 minors. Peer-reviewed research describes the US military-basing economy around Clark as sustaining sexual markets that disproportionately exploit poor transgender Filipina women, and the 2024 US Trafficking in Persons Report confirms traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas around the country.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the venues where trans women are concentrated in commercial sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. No protective ordinance cluster comparable to the capital region or Central Visayas is documented here.

sources.claim: US government Trafficking in Persons Report 2024, Philippines chapter (archived site): traffickers exploit victims in tourist destinations and urban areas around the country. (Cached fetch returned only the archive-page chrome; summary from the research dossier line.)

sources.title: NBI dismantles human trafficking operation in Angeles City; rescues 45 victims, including 13 minors (NBI press release, 17 June 2025)
sources.claim: National Bureau of Investigation press release (17 June 2025): on 1 June 2025 the NBI Bataan District Office arrested Alvin Baguio, the registered owner of Field Sensation's Bar, together with four others (Reden Roa, John Parro, Shirly Calilong, Marilyn Ferrer) engaged in human trafficking in Barangay Balibago, Angeles City, following a 19 May 2025 referral from Destiny Rescue Pilipinas Incorporated; agents ran an entrapment and rescue operation in which 'barfine' transactions ranged from P5,000 to P10,000, and 45 victims including 13 minors were rescued and turned over to the social welfare agency. Government-source confirmation of the June 2025 Field Sensation's Bar dismantling in Angeles City that anchors this record's trafficking-enforcement claim for Central Luzon.

sources.title: NBI arrests a foreign national for human trafficking; rescues 12 trafficked victims including 5 minors (NBI press release, 10 March 2025)
sources.claim: National Bureau of Investigation press release (10 March 2025): the NBI Bataan District Office arrested foreign national Shin Ki Jung and accomplices in Angeles City, Pampanga for violations of R.A. No. 11862 (Expanded Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2022) and R.A. No. 7610; a complaint from the husband of a trafficked victim alleged women were recruited as Korea-bound performers as cover for working at a club in Angeles City, and a subsequent rescue operation freed 12 victims including 5 minors, with the arrested subjects presented for inquest before the Office of the City Prosecutor of Angeles City. Government-source confirmation of the record's March 2025 Angeles City anti-trafficking arrest with the same victim and minor counts.

sources.title: In Philippine red-light district, an uphill struggle to battle trafficking and abuses (Preda Foundation / The Fuller Project, 21 November 2019)
sources.claim: Preda Foundation article (published 21 November 2019, originally The Fuller Project's reporting): hundreds of girls are supplied each year in Angeles City to meet demand from foreign men paying for sex, many of them American, in the city that hosted a former US military base; more than 150 women and girls interviewed by The Fuller Project in Angeles City said they wanted to leave prostitution but did not know how; city-regulated 'entertainers' must take weekly STD tests, which activists criticised as marketing the sex industry as clean, and advocates warned that a new airport terminal on the city's outskirts could triple visitor numbers and expand sex trafficking. Structural documentation of the Central Luzon red-light economy that this record identifies as the region's principal traveler-facing risk.

records.name: Calabarzon
records.current_summary:
This region surrounds the national capital without sharing its protective ordinances: none is documented here, and the visitor picture is the national one — killings of trans women without dependable local machinery.

Against that backdrop, in August 2025 a newly crowned LGBTQ pageant winner was found dead with 13 stab wounds in a city south of the capital, days after the crowning, and police worked the killing as a homicide case — a high-signal violent episode for this region's record.

sources.claim: Philippine daily report (13 August 2025): LGBTQ pageant winner murdered in Batangas — the Lipa City finding with 13 stab wounds days after the crowning, worked as a homicide case. (Publisher returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; summary from the research dossier line.)

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in the Philippines - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Philippines country overview documents the national framework behind this region's record: there is no national anti-discrimination law - the SOGIE Equality Bill has been proposed since the 2000s and failed to pass, and in November 2022 the newly elected government rejected United Nations recommendations including passage of the bill as "unacceptable" - and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender. The page lists local anti-discrimination ordinances, several inside Calabarzon: Batangas province (2015), Cavite (2014-2018, later extended to cover gender identity), Batangas City (2016) and Calamba (2017), and it records that murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons in the Philippines have been reported since at least 2012.

records.name: Cagayan Valley
records.current_summary: On 31 July 2024 in Ilagan City, Isabela, Morine "G." Cabansag, 40, was found dead in a cemetery after an alleged kidnapping and rape in Centro San Antonio; three suspects were identified. The monitored trans-murder count records the cause as stabbing. This is one of six documented killings of trans women in eighteen months in the national series, with arrests made in at least three of them and none reported prosecuted to conviction. No protective ordinance, institutional-hostility finding or enforcement pattern specific to trans visitors is documented in this region beyond this single incident.

sources.claim: Trans-murder monitoring project report: the Cabansag killing in Ilagan City, Isabela, 31 July 2024, stabbed, following alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects identified. (Report page verified from the fetched record listing.)

sources.title: Recent killings of trans women prompt groups to push for LGBTQIA protection (Bulatlat)
sources.claim: Bulatlat, 26 June 2025, reports that 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol (formerly Gian Molina), a business management student at Cagayan State University resident in Zone 7, Centro, Peñablanca, Cagayan, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025, days after being reported missing; her mother told local media (95.7 XFM Tuguegarao) she saw visible signs of physical assault when the body was found. A criminology student of the University of Cagayan Valley, named online as 'Menco de Guzman'/'Sherwin Kyqle', voluntarily surrendered to the Peñablanca police station, admitting he picked Kierra up on Saturday night but denying involvement. Bahaghari chairperson Reyna Valmores Salinas called the killing proof that LGBTQ+ persons remain unsafe and renewed the call for the SOGIESC Equality Bill (House Bill No. 5551; Senate Bill No. 1600), noting no national anti-discrimination law has passed in 25 years. Documents a second trans-woman killing inside Cagayan Valley (Cagayan province) within the 2024-2025 national series this record tracks, with an identified suspect who surrendered to police.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ groups, umalma sa ikalawang tala ng pamamaslang sa estudyanteng trans woman (Manila Today)
sources.claim: Manila Today, 25 June 2025 (Filipino), reports that two days after Kierra Apostol was reported missing, the trans woman student — an incoming first-year Business Management student at Cagayan State University-Caritan Campus and a hair-and-makeup artist active in local gay pageants — was found floating in the river between Amulung and Iguig in Cagayan on the morning of 23 June 2025, her mother citing marks of violence. LGBTQIA+ groups including CSU Crystal (Cagayan State University-Andrew campus), LGBT Pilipinas Taguig City Inc. and Bahaghari chair Reyna Valmores Salinas demanded a full and thorough investigation, justice, and immediate passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Independent corroboration of the second documented trans-woman killing in this region, adding the Amulung-Iguig river location and the suspect-surrender detail beyond the Bulatlat account.

records.name: Western Visayas
records.current_summary:
On 10 October 2022 the Capiz State University Office of Student Affairs told students perceived as trans women that they would be barred from university premises unless they cut their hair and wore the uniform prescribed for males, delivering the instruction through campus guards with one week to comply and threatening that they could not re-enroll otherwise; the office attributed the order to the university president. A legal-NGO case study documents the students' subsequent advocacy campaign — backed by paralegals of national LGBTQ organisations, who pointed to an existing municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Roxas City, Capiz, which the office dismissed as inapplicable — and its later milestone: the first openly trans woman graduating as university valedictorian with highest honours. This is a documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing in a provincial (not metropolitan) setting, reversed by advocacy.

No killings from the 2024-2025 national series occurred in this region. The campus directive is a resident-facing action rather than a mechanism a visitor encounters; its force as a region signal is that in a conservative provincial setting expression can be policed by institutional authority without an operational local recourse — unlike Central Visayas, this region has no protective ordinance cluster of comparable reach.
records.current_localsOnly: The documented gender-expression policing (the 2022 Capiz State University directive) applied to enrolled students, not visitors.

sources.claim: Legal-NGO case study (December 2025): the October 2022 Capiz State University exclusion of students perceived as trans women, the advocacy response, and the later valedictorian milestone. (Article body verified from the fetched copy.)

sources.title: Trans woman makes history as she graduates summa cum laude from Capiz State U (Inquirer.net)
sources.claim: Inquirer.net, 7 August 2025, reports that at its 21st commencement exercises Capiz State University produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude — Khaz-JP Padilla, batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honor — the outcome this record attributes to the Capiz State advocacy campaign that followed the October 2022 hair-and-uniform directive. Padilla describes the school's binary haircut rules she faced in earlier years ('Why is it that whenever I cut my hair... it feels like I'm losing my self-confidence?') and her transition once pandemic-era online classes freed her from the haircut rule. Confirms the 'first openly trans woman graduating as valedictorian with highest honours' milestone claimed in the record. Page verified via a Wayback Machine snapshot of 5 January 2026; the live Inquirer.net URL is Cloudflare-gated.

records.name: Ilocos Region
records.current_summary:
The Pangasinan provincial board certified and affirmed Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 of Bayambang protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons (Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024, session of 19 August 2024)—a provincial-level endorsement of a municipal LGBTQ+ protection ordinance in a conservative province. This gives a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor a local complaint route absent in most other regions.

Against that, the Abra and Ilocos Sur provinces within Ilocos Region host the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group (BIAG), a codified customary-justice system with its own dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences," recognised by Philippine courts. No trans-specific bodong ruling or customary exclusion was documented, but the legal-pluralism structure means that in a rural Abra or Ilocos Sur dispute, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

Net effect: +0.03 above the national score, modest because the protective ordinance is municipal and the plural-justice uncertainty is localized to specific provinces within the region. Compare Central Visayas (0.63), where the ordinance cluster is broader (city IRRs with UNDP backing, unanimous municipal votes) and there is no countervailing alternative-justice structure.

sources.claim: Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024, adopted at the Pangasinan Sangguniang Panlalawigan session of 19 August 2024 (Lingayen): the board declared Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 of the Sangguniang Bayan of Bayambang — an ordinance protecting lesbians, gays, bisexuals, transgenders, queers and intersex in Bayambang against all forms of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics (SOGIESC), with penalties for violation — conforms with the Bill of Rights and Section 16, R.A. No. 7160 (Local Government Code 1991). The resolution is a provincial-level endorsement affirming a municipal anti-discrimination ordinance, giving LGBTQI persons a local legal complaint route in the Pangasinan corridor.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (403 anti-bot; zero-length extract); the underlying journal article documents the bodong customary-justice system as a judicial institution — adopted and modified by Itneg elders in Abra and Ilocos Sur (now the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group) as an alternative dispute-resolution body operating alongside Philippine courts and police.

sources.title: Municipal Ordinance No. 15, Series of 2023, Municipality of Bayambang, Pangasinan — An Ordinance Protecting the Rights of Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, Transgenders, Queers and Intersex (LGBTQI) in the Municipality of Bayambang Against Any and All Forms of Discrimination Solely on the Basis of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, Expression, Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC) and Providing Penalties for Violation Thereof (certified copy)
sources.claim: The certified eight-page copy of Bayambang Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, protects LGBTQI persons in the municipality against discrimination 'solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression, sex characteristics (SOGIESC)' and sets a penalty ladder: first offence a fine of at least Php1,000 or one month's imprisonment; second offence at least Php2,000 or one month-and-a-day to six months; third offence at least Php2,500 or six months-and-a-day to eight months; later violations one year's imprisonment plus at least Php2,500; violators must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay (Katarungang Pambarangay) mechanism under R.A. 7160, giving a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor an actual local complaint route. This is the operative municipal instrument endorsed provincially by the Pangasinan Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024 cited in the record's existing source.

sources.title: Municipal Ordinances — Municipality of Bayambang (official registry of the Sangguniang Bayan)
sources.claim: The official registry of the Municipality of Bayambang lists Ordinance No. 15-2023, 'An Ordinance Protecting the Rights of Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, Transgenders, Queers and Intersex (LGBTQI) in the Municipality of Bayambang Against Any and All Forms of Discrimination Solely on the Basis of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, Expression, Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC) and Providing Penalties for Violation Thereof,' as authored by Hon. Confirms the number, series, author and enactment date this record cites for Bayambang's local protective ordinance.

records.name: ARMM
records.current_summary:
In the Bangsamoro autonomous region justice is legally plural: the region's 2019 administrative code provides that it be dispensed in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, and traditional or tribal laws (the clause is carried in the research dossier; the cached code excerpt does not reach it), while the national Code of Muslim Personal Laws of 1977 remains in force. In July 2026 the Bangsamoro parliament tabled a bill for a comprehensive Shari'ah justice system code extending to ta'zir criminal offences — the category under which morality offences are prosecuted in comparable systems. No source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no such law has yet passed.

The Shari'ah court system is expanding nationally: three new judicial districts and twelve circuit courts beyond BARMM were created by law signed in August 2024, extending into majority-Christian areas, with further access legislation in September 2025 and a Supreme Court resolution in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.

The finding for a trans visitor is structural rather than enforcement-based: a dispute could fall outside the civil courts altogether, in a jurisdiction actively legislating criminal religious law with no protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure documented in the region. Forward-looking, and bounded by the fact that the ta'zir code is a proposal, not a power in force.

sources.claim: Full text of Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13 (the Bangsamoro Administrative Code), begun 29 March 2019, from the Bangsamoro Official Gazette: prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region (cached extract covers the introductory provisions; the code's justice-dispensation clause — 'in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws' — is cited in the dossier), while guaranteeing religious freedom.

Bangsamoro Parliament (2026-07-14): proposed Shari'ah Justice Code — 10 books extending Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status law confined since PD 1083 (1977) into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and ADR; rests on BOL authority and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. For the record: marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums with written-opt-in clauses for civil entities — the legal-pluralist marriage regime a visitor's Muslim spouse-status questions would run through.

Christianity Today (2024-11): August 2024, President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; parliament passed it unanimously. For the record: dated confirmation that Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime is expanding nationally, with local Christian-leader reaction.
